title: Police feared lives at risk
article: It was a lively exchange that punctuated the second day of an ongoing inquest into the 2009 death of Phillip Jeffrey Charbonneau in an incident with OPP officers on County Road 29.
Const. Ross Dennison was on the scene July 3, 2009 with other officers who had Charbonneau's black pickup truck blocked in along the highway near Forthton.
As Dennison took the stand Tuesday, Lawrence Greenspon, the lawyer for Charbonneau's family, grilled him about why a pair of other officers opened fire.
"I believed the driver was trying to run down the other officers," Dennison said.

But Greenspon argued that in earlier testimony, Dennison had said that when he first arrived at the scene, Charbonneau looked like he was ramming the police cruisers with his truck for the purpose of trying to move left, toward an opening where he could escape.
"Twenty minutes ago, you said he was trying to move one way to get out of there," Greenspon said.

Day Two of the coroner's inquest into Charbonneau's death brought several notable exchanges between Greenspon and lawyers for the OPP, as well as testimony from several officers involved in the pursuit that night.

Several key questions came up frequently throughout the day, including the time frame between Charbonneau being stopped at a Reduce Impaired Driving Everywhere (RIDE) check at the westbound Highway 401 Brockville off-ramp at approximately 11:02 p.m. and the report at approximately 11:07 p.m. to the OPP communications centre of shots being fired.

In particular, Greenspon questioned Sgt. Chris Watkins about the length of time between the report by officers back to the OPP communications centre that Charbonneau was ramming their vehicles and the shots being fired.
According to the transcript of the audio, Greenspon noted, this was a span of seven seconds.
However Watkins cautioned that the transcript only shows the seconds between communication times, not necessarily the real time lapsed between the two events.
"We have to be careful ... there was seven seconds between communication times," Watkins said, adding that treating the transcript times like real times means making a "dangerous inference."

Greenspon also questioned Watkins, who that night was communicating by radio with the other officers from the OPP's Smiths Falls communication centre in his role as a communications sergeant, as to why officers were given the go-ahead to engage in the high-speed pursuit that followed when all that was known at that point was that Charbonneau had "blown through a RIDE check."
"My experience as a police officer tells me that when someone doesn't stop at a RIDE check, there's reason to believe they are impaired," Watkins responded.
Also taking the stand separately on Tuesday was Const. Michael Benn, a veteran OPP officer of more than 30 years.

Under questioning from Crown Attorney Robert Wadden, Benn recounted details of the pursuit and the scene where Charbonneau was hemmed in by other cruisers after having hit a spike belt laid by Dennison a few moments earlier.

Unable to get out of his car due to being parked alongside Charbonneau's truck and having the large onboard computer system the OPP uses in its cars to his right, Benn said he was left with little choice but to take cover when he heard shots ring out.
"I was unable to get out of the line of fire, so I ducked down," he said.

Under questioning from Greeenspon, Benn, who said he had never encountered this type of standoff in his career up to that point, also said his concern was that Charbonneau was going to run down one of the other officers who were outside their vehicles.
"I was thinking, if this guy doesn't stop, he's going to kill somebody," Benn said.
But Greenspon questioned whether Benn heard any officers warn Charbonneau that they would shoot if he did not stop ramming the cruisers.
Benn said he heard something along the lines of "get out" from the officers, but said that with the noise at the scene, it might have been easy to mishear the other officers' words.
"At the same time, there was a lot of noise from the sirens," Benn said.

Tuesday's proceedings also included a significant amount of testimony by officers about the deployment of spike belts during pursuits, as well as questions from Greenspon as to what other methods could have been used to avoid the shooting.
"Did you have pepper spray with you that night,?" Greenspon asked Dennison.
After Dennison responded that he did, Greenspon asked if he ever considered using it, to which he replied he did not because he didn't feel that it was a safe situation in which to try it.

Dennison also fielded a similar question from one of the jurors, who asked if officers might have been able to "take out" the back tires of Charbonneau's truck -meaning all four would have been disabled, as the front two were punctured by the spike belt - so that he couldn't escape once he was stopped.
"The vehicle would still have been able to move," Dennison said.

In another key piece of testimony, Dennison also told the inquest, under questioning from Norm Feaver, a lawyer for the OPP and the Ministry of Community Safety and Correctional Services, that he felt there wasn't any doubt that Charbonneau could see that officers had their guns drawn when he was warned by officers to stop moving his vehicle.
"Is there any doubt in your mind that he was able to observe guns drawn on him?" Feaver asked.
"Not at all, sir," Dennison responded.

The Special Investigations Unit (SIU), a civilian agency that investigates deaths or serious injuries involving the police, cleared the two officers they investigated in relation to Charbonneau's death, saying there was reason to believe the officers' testimony that they believed their lives were in danger that night.
The current inquest, overseen by Coroner Dr. David Evans, is taking place before a jury of four women and one man.

The purpose of the inquest, as laid out on Monday by Evans, is to establish the "five Ws" -who, what, where, when and by what means - relating to Charbonneau's death, as well as looking into possible recommendations to avoid a similar tragedy in the future.
The inquest is expected to last 10 days and feature testimony from more than 20 witnesses.
Proceedings continue today at the Leeds and Grenville County Courthouse in Brockville.
